clinical_targets.goal: Complete alleviation of primary presenting complaint and systemic stability
Return of baseline physiological parameters (vital signs, CBC, metabolic panel)
Full return to activities of daily living (ADLs) and functional autonomy

Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Cannabis focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Cannabis.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Cannabis require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Cannabis.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Calculate CrCl using Cockcroft-Gault before prescribing narrow therapeutic index drugs.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Review patient's complete prescription and OTC medication list for drug-induced liver injury (DILI).
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Verify safety in pregnancy and lactation databases before prescribing any new therapeutic class.
special_populations.elderly: Perform medication reconciliation to eliminate unnecessary polypharmacy and anticholinergic load.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is cannabis? Cannabis, also known as marijuana, is a green, brown, or gray mixture of dried parts from the cannabis plant. The plant contains chemicals that affect the brain and can change how you feel or think. The main active chemicals are cannabinoids, including: THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), which causes the "high" CBD (cannabidiol), which does not cause a high How do people use cannabis? There are many ways that people use cannabis, including: Rolling it up and smoking it like a cigarette ("joint") or cigar ("blunt") Smoking it in a pipe ("bowl") or water pipe ("bong") Mixing it into drinks like tea, or food like cakes or brownies ("edibles") Smoking concentrated oils ("dabbing") Using electronic vaporizers ("vaping") Taking liquid drops under the tongue ("tinctures") Applying it to the skin as lotions or balms ("topicals") Topical products usually do not cause a high. What are the effects of cannabis? Cannabis can cause short-term and long-term effects. These can vary depending on: How much you use How often you use it The THC level The ingredients How you take it Other medicines or drugs used at the same time Other health conditions you have Your age and sex Your experience with cannabis Short-term effects: While you are high, you may notice: Changes in senses, such as seeing brighter colors Altered sense of time, such as minutes seeming like hours Changes in mood Problems with body movement Trouble with thinking, problem-solving, and memory Increased appetite Slower reaction time Secondhand smoke from cannabis products has many of the same risks as secondhand tobacco smoke . Long-term effects: In the long term, cannabis can cause health problems, which can include: Problems with brain development. People who started using cannabis as teenagers may have trouble with thinking, memory, and learning. Coughing and breathing problems, if you smoke cannabis frequently. Repeated episodes of nausea, vomiting , and stomach pain due to long-term, heavy cannabis use. This is called cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS). Problems with fetal and child development during and after pregnancy, if you smoke cannabis while pregnant . Heavy long-term use of cannabis has been linked to increased risk of cancer , digestive issues , heart problems , and mental health problems . Can you overdose on cannabis? It is possible to overdose on cannabis, if you take a very high dose. You may feel anxious or panicked or have a rapid heartbeat . In rare cases, an overdose can cause paranoia and hallucinations. There are no reports of people dying from just using cannabis. Is cannabis addictive? Cannabis can be addictive . THC levels in products have increased over time. Stronger products raise the risk of addiction, known as cannabis use disorder. You are more likely to become addicted if you use cannabis every day or started using it when you were a teenager. When you try to quit, you may have mild withdrawal symptoms such as: Irritability Trouble sleeping Decreased appetite Anxiety Cravings What is medical cannabis? The cannabis plant contains chemicals that may help with some health problems, but it's not clear if the whole plant can treat or cure them. Recreational cannabis is still illegal under federal law. Federal rules have eased somewhat for medical cannabis and FDA-approved cannabis drugs. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved man-made forms of THC. These drugs treat nausea caused by chemotherapy and increase appetite in people with certain health conditions who have lost a lot of weight. There is also a liquid drug that contains CBD. It treats three forms of severe childhood epilepsy . Researchers are studying whether cannabis and its ingredients may treat more conditions. Most U.S. states allow medical cannabis, and about half also allow recreational use for adults 21 and older. NIH: National Institute on Drug Abuse
style_3_monograph.treatment: Treatment and care involves: Preventing injury Reassuring those who have panic reactions due to the drug Sedatives, called benzodiazepines, such as diazepam (Valium) or lorazepam (Ativan), may be given. Children who have more serious symptoms or those with serious side effects may need to stay in the hospital for treatment. Treatment may include heart and brain monitoring. In the emergency department, the person may receive: Activated charcoal, if the drug has been eaten Blood and urine tests Breathing support, including oxygen, tube through the mouth, and breathing machine (ventilator) Chest x-ray CT scan Electrocardiogram (ECG) Fluids through the vein (intravenous, or IV) Medicines to relieve symptoms (see above)
